summary: Defines requirements for DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) protocols that enable coordinated response to distributed denial-of-service attacks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: DOTS lets one network ask another for help responding to a distributed denial-of-service attack. RFC 8612 defines requirements for the signaling, bulk data exchange, and security of future DOTS protocols.

questions: what is dots ddos open threat signaling
what are the dots signal channel requirements
what is the dots data channel
subtitle: Requirements for resilient signaling between networks coordinating a DDoS response.

tldr.problem: DDoS mitigation services often use proprietary interfaces, limiting coordination among subscribers, providers, and other network operators. The interface may also need to work while an attack congests the network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies requirements for a resilient signal channel for mitigation requests and status, a separate reliable data channel for bulk configuration, security, and a shared data model.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8612 is an Informational requirements document, not a DOTS protocol. It leaves the mitigation method itself outside scope.

today: RFC 8612 is an Informational requirements document, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It specifies requirements for DOTS protocols and data models rather than defining a protocol itself.

sections.title: Why Standardized DDoS Signaling Is Needed
sections.content:
Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks can saturate network links. Enterprises that lack the resources to mitigate attacks themselves may use provider traffic-scrubbing services, which try to separate attack traffic from legitimate traffic.

The RFC says these services used proprietary interfaces, which tied subscribers to particular services and limited coordination with other network elements. DDoS Open Threat Signaling (DOTS) communicates the need for defensive action before or during an attack, but it does not specify how mitigation is performed.
sections.plainLanguage: A network under attack may need a service provider or another network to help filter traffic. DOTS is meant to provide a common way to request and coordinate that help.

sections.title: DOTS Agents and Channels
sections.content:
A DOTS client requests attack-response coordination. A DOTS server handles the request, asks a mitigator to act when needed, and returns selected feedback. A DOTS gateway combines client and server roles to connect downstream clients with upstream servers.

The signal channel is bidirectional and mutually authenticated, and is intended to remain useful despite severe packet loss. The separate data channel carries infrequent, reliable bulk exchanges and is not expected to work during congestion. A drop-list identifies sources to block; an accept-list identifies sources that should always be allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: The client requests help, the server coordinates the request, and a mitigator applies countermeasures. DOTS uses a small signal channel for urgent messages and a separate data channel for bulk information.

sections.title: General Requirements
sections.content:
DOTS protocols and data models must be extensible and backward compatible. Older implementations must ignore optional information they do not understand and reject messages that contain mandatory information they cannot process.

The signal protocol must keep operating despite loss, duplication, or out-of-order delivery, and should minimize message size and connection overhead. A separate secure channel using reliable transport must carry bulk data. Clients may send mitigation hints, but servers may ignore them. Implementations should also detect and end loops caused by configuration or routing errors.
sections.plainLanguage: The signaling must continue to work when messages are lost, repeated, or reordered during an attack. Large configuration exchanges use a separate reliable channel, and future versions must handle older implementations predictably.

sections.title: Signal Channel Requirements
sections.content:
The signal channel should use connectionless transport such as UDP; TCP may be used when network policy or middleboxes require it. Messages must fit below the path MTU, including security and transport overhead. If the path MTU is unknown, agents must assume 1280 bytes, with 576 bytes optionally used for IPv4.

The channel must be bidirectional and agents must exchange heartbeats to monitor health and keep NAT or firewall bindings alive. During active mitigation, agents should avoid ending the channel merely because heartbeats are lost, since attack traffic can cause packet loss.

Authorized clients must be able to request scoped mitigation, receive status and rejection reasons, inspect blocked-packet and byte metrics, and withdraw requests. Requests include a lifetime and can be renewed. The active-but-terminating period may be extended up to 300 seconds to dampen rapid changes. Required scopes include IPv4 prefixes, IPv6 prefixes, and domain names; URIs are optional.
sections.plainLanguage: Signal messages must be small enough to avoid fragmentation, and the channel must remain active through packet loss during mitigation. Each request names what to protect and how long mitigation should last, and the server reports its status.

sections.title: Bulk Data and the Shared Data Model
sections.content:
The data channel supports configuration and bulk exchange that does not fit the small signal messages. It must deliver messages reliably and in order. Examples include configuring resource identifiers and managing drop-lists and accept-lists.

The DOTS data model must be versioned and able to represent mitigation requests and withdrawals, scope, lifetime, status and failure reasons, perceived efficacy, heartbeat preferences, and acceptable signal loss. The data model must not assume a specific transport's properties.
sections.plainLanguage: The data channel reliably carries larger configuration items, such as lists of sources to block or allow. The shared data model describes what a request protects, how long it lasts, and what status the server reports.

sections.title: Security and Operational Risks
sections.content:
DOTS agents must authenticate each other and protect messages for confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity using secure transports such as TLS or DTLS. Protocols must detect and prevent replay, and servers must authorize client messages about mitigation, configuration, filtering, and status.

The RFC warns that an impersonated client could cause a server to install drop-lists that block inbound traffic, while an impersonated server could discard mitigation requests. Blocking the signal channel can also disrupt the core request for help. Operators should monitor and audit DOTS agents. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must prove their identity, protect messages, and reject replays. Otherwise an attacker could misuse a request to block legitimate traffic or prevent mitigation from being applied.
